title: Three Treasures
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny's talk highlights the importance of not defaming or diminishing the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha in our lives, a precept often misunderstood as simply avoiding criticism of these concepts. Instead, it's about cultivating a genuine understanding of what it means to take refuge in them and developing an authentic practice that allows us to see their true nature within ourselves. By letting go of cynicism and doubt, we can deepen our connection with the Buddhist teachings and open ourselves up to the present moment, embracing the world as it is without trying to fit everything into a set of teachings.

sentences.text: Good evening.
I'm going to be talking tonight on the 10th precept, not defaming the three treasures.
We've been going through these talks about the precepts for, I don't know, a couple of months now.
We haven't done them particularly in their numerical order, but I think this is the last one.
Is this right?
A summary talk, yeah.
It also happens to be the actual last precept, so by whatever chance, that's the way it's worked out.
I did a little different approach to the talk this time.
A lot of times when I've done talks in the past, I've written them out completely.
And I thought, I really need to be more spontaneous, so I decided to do the low-preparation end of the talk.
It shouldn't take long, right?
I wanted to show you some books I was using.
These are books that some other people have shown.
I haven't been around for all the talks, so I don't know if all these books have been discussed before.
But *The Mind of Clover* by Robert Aitken, which most people have definitely been referring to, is an excellent book.
For me personally, it was a really important book when I encountered it many years ago.
I read it, and when I got to the last page, I just flipped it over and started reading it again from the beginning.
I think I did that three times.
Reb Anderson's *Being Upright* is a very, very heartfelt, deep book about the precepts, and it's really recommended.
There's also [unclear: "Daning Categories"], *Returning to Silence*, which includes a section related to the precepts.
I really enjoy this book because it's just absorbing.
You sort of lose yourself in it, and you can pick it up at any point.
And also [unclear: "A Teeth Not Haunts"] *the Heart of the Buddhist Teachings*, which includes a section about precepts and many other Buddhist-based teachings.
So I dipped into these books, but decided that the presentation of upright sitting in our lives is really the expression of the Three Treasures.
That's the heart of one of the points I'd like to make.
There's a quote here from Reb Anderson, where he discusses Suzuki Roshi's way of presenting the Three Treasures in his life.
Reb says,
*Suzuki Roshi often said that his main job as a Zen priest was to encourage people to practice upright sitting.
This was his primary way of protecting and sustaining the Triple Treasure.
For him, the most pure and direct way of sustaining the Buddha treasure was just to be fully himself in each moment.
His way of protecting the Dharma treasure was to practice wholeheartedly with no gaining idea.
And his way of protecting and sustaining the Sangha treasure was what he called group practice, practicing together in harmony, which he upheld even to the detriment of his physical health.*
So in that sense, Suzuki Roshi, by maintaining his own sitting practice, is being a Buddha.
So he's upholding the taking refuge in Buddha.
By not thinking of any gaining idea in what he's doing, he's continually practicing giving and the Dharma.
And by practicing with others and helping others sustain their practices, he's practicing Sangha.

It's important, I think, when we're looking at the precepts, to remember, and I'm not sure if any of the other speakers have mentioned this before, a sort of, and I think this is a bit of a classical interpretation of the precepts, three-pronged approach to viewing each precept.
You could call it a Buddha-Dharma-Sangha approach, but it would be a universal approach, an absolute approach and a relative approach.
So say, for instance, in the precept of not killing, or protecting life, a universal approach would be that there is no killing, nothing is born, nothing dies.
An absolute approach would say, don't kill.
And a relativistic approach would be, sometimes life passes and we have to be aware of the need for these things to happen.
Each one of these isn't really a very complete understanding of the precept, but the three of them together are the way in which we hold the precept and practice with it.
This can be applied to each of the precepts, in a way.
But the ground of the precepts, the way in which you enter, is in the process of taking refuge, which is common to most every Buddhist school.
As you'll notice, in the ceremony of Jukai, in which a student takes the Buddhist precepts, the beginning of that ceremonial process is the taking of refuge.
That works on through the three pure precepts and then these ten precepts that we've been having talks about.
The final precept, the one I'm discussing tonight, has been variously called different things.
Sometimes the precepts are worded in a negative fashion and sometimes in a positivistic fashion.
More classically, it's been in a negativistic fashion.
In this sense, I think that with this precept it's useful to use that wording, in contrast to the taking of refuge.
So not defaming the three treasures is a corollary practice to taking refuge in the three treasures.
What would it mean to not defame the three treasures if you're trying to take refuge in them?
This gives you a sense of a way to practice with the three treasures and understand them better.
To understand that, you first have to have a bit of a sense about the taking of refuge.
The taking of refuge is a sense of going home to your essential self and your essential understanding of the world and how things are.
In that sense, it's sometimes put as: I go back to the Buddha in myself.
I take refuge in the Buddha.
I go back to the Dharma in myself.
These might be some ways to understand the spirit of the taking of refuge.
And of the three, Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, the taking of refuge in Buddha encompasses all.
You need to perhaps think that this has different levels of connotation.
We can think about the Buddha as the historical Buddha, the teacher who founded these teachings that we are practicing.
We can also think of Buddha as a quality, some sort of universal quality, unexplainable.
Is it an energy?
Is it a thing?
Is it an "it"?
Is it definable?
But it is a macro view, as opposed to the micro view of looking at it as, oh, that was a person.
It's the same thing with the Dharma.
It can be the Buddhist teachings.
But it can also be the world and the functionings of the world, the minute and myriad and ultimately completely unknowable functionings of the world.
We grasp at it as humans, especially with our scientific understanding, to try and understand the world.
But ultimately, we're really at the tip of a very large iceberg.
The way in which things work and fit together in this world is somehow vast and perhaps beyond what we're going to be able to figure out ultimately.
And then the sangha, the Buddhist sangha, which we are.
We could say there's a collective sangha of Buddhists everywhere.
But the sangha is every being, everything that can be called a being, in their interaction, in their relationships, in their relational sense.
Sangha is about relation, about being intimate in relationships with each other and in the idea that nothing really exists alone.
That's the heart of the sangha.
So in not defaming the three treasures, what is that really all about?
It's often been a precept that tripped me up.
I thought, well, of course I wouldn't.
Why are they even saying that?
It might be the same thing with other precepts for other people, like, say, the precept of not lying.
You might think, well, I never lie.
It's interesting to talk about it, but I think this other precept over here is something I'm having some trouble with.
Maybe I'll work with that one.
But all precepts equally, I think, have much to teach us if we start looking under the surface of them.
And not defaming the three treasures, and thinking about that word, it's obviously translated from some other word, but it means making them less than they really are in our lives.
This is an easy trap to fall into.
It's objectifying the Buddha, or even our sense of what Buddha nature might be, making it something outside of ourselves.
We often hear in Zen that story of Lin Chi, who would say, if you meet the Buddha on the road, kill him, which always sounds like such a catchy, quirky Zen thing to say.
What does that really mean?
Does it mean, reject doctrine or something like that?
But what I think it really means is, if you see the Buddha, you're objectifying the Buddha.
The Buddha is outside of you.
You need to allow that thought to perish and realize that the Buddha is within you and within all beings.
So with this sense about defaming the three treasures, you can see how, if you work with it, it can have a pretty deep resonance.

You can see that there's quite a long way you can go, where you realize, I'm really not extending my sense of what the Dharma is in my life and in the life of this world, or what the Sangha really is.
I'm holding a narrow view of it.
And when you hold a narrow view of it, you're defaming it for what it really is.
That is what this precept, I think, is very much about.
Aitken Roshi, throughout his book here, *The Mind of Clover*, goes back to two different commentary threads throughout his discussion of all the precepts.
One of the commentary threads is from Dogen Zenji, the founder of our sect.
For this precept, his quote from Dogen is typically Dogen, something that at first seems to hit you sideways, and you wonder if he's even talking about the subject you think he's talking about.
Dogen Zenji said,
*So this is the teaching that's presented in what we really are, our actualness.
And that is both the resting place and the place of catching the teachings, the harbor and the weir.
Its virtue finds its home in the ocean of essential nature.
And it's beyond explanation, just accepting it with respect and gratitude.*
We're alive, and we didn't do that.

We really need to respect the fact that we are alive, and that we live in this world, and that this world is something that is here, that we didn't create, but in all of its wonderfulness, we are within it.
To not appreciate all of that for its fullness of what it really is, is to lessen it, to define it.
What this really comes down to is an exploration, within our precept practice, of what faith is in a Buddhist context.

That doesn't mean some sort of rigid faith in a doctrinaire approach to life, where everything needs to be fit into a set of teachings that we understand and anything outside of that gets disregarded.
That's not what I'm talking about.
What I'm talking about is a continual opening, where you have to trust, have faith, that your life is really the life that you are supposed to be having, and that you do have right now, every moment.
And this world is the world that we're in, the way it functions.
To really embrace that is the faith that is inherent in Buddhist practice.
To practice that is to come to terms, to come to face, with a certain inner, ever-present cynicism that is part of being a human being.
A certain doubt about whether there's any meaning to your life, any sense of organization or connectedness to your life.
It's really present just within the human condition to have that cynicism.
It's just there.
Part of it is that tendency to objectify things, to reduce them, to narrow their meaning.
When you see yourself doing that around something, that points up to you that, oh, here's a place where I could be more open to the three treasures.
So that is what I've come up with to try and explain this.
I think that when we practice with the precepts, we are always taking them anew, coming at them from a fresh angle again.
I hope that what I've had to say helps a little bit in understanding this.
Thank you.
